teaser.text: Realty Income is a landlord whose product is access to commercial property, packaged as rent-paying contracts with businesses. To follow a dollar through the company, start with the buildings it owns, then trace the rent through tenants, lease renewals, financing, and distributions.

stock.title: Realty Income stock forecast
stock.meta_description: Realty Income stock forecast: the weighted case reaches $60.87 by October 2029, with bear, base and bull scenarios.
stock.opening: Realty Income's weighted case is $60.87 in October 2029, with bear, base and bull probabilities of 30%, 55% and 15%. Realty Income's outcome hinges on per-share cash growth after funding costs and dilution.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains Realty Income's business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Realty Income's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The forecast points to modest total returns, with the base case producing the most likely path. The weighted price is $57.73 in October 2027, a 9% return including dividends. It rises to $59.18 in October 2028, a 17% return. By October 2029, it reaches $60.87, a 27% return.

The final-date outcomes are much wider: the bear case reaches $48.29, while the bull case reaches $81.52. Today’s reference price is $56.08. The bear, base and bull probabilities are 30%, 55% and 15%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right—and what could go wrong for Realty Income?

paragraphs.text: The base case applies 6% annual total AFFO growth, reaching $4,409 million, $4,674 million and $4,954 million. It assumes guidance-level execution, continued investment and partner capital. The bear case uses 2% growth because debt costs, dilution and weaker new-client reletting could absorb most acquisition growth. The bull case uses 9% because cheaper funding, attractive acquisition spreads and partner-funded expansion could accelerate results. AFFO rose every year from 2021 through 2025, but per-share growth was slower when issuance was heavy.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Realty Income really make?

paragraphs.text: AFFO estimates recurring earnings capacity after company-defined adjustments to FFO. Those adjustments include items such as straight-line rent, leasing costs, credit losses, and debt-cost amortization. The per-share figure matters because it reflects the share count. The payout table shows a dividend below AFFO, leaving room under Realty Income’s formula.

Property spending also deserves inspection. Realty Income spent $131.8 million on real-estate improvements, including leasing costs, while its AFFO bridge deducted $9.8 million for leasing costs and recurring capital expenditures. Some improvements may support growth, but some property needs recur in practice. The specialist therefore treats the payout as a coverage signal, not as proof that the remainder is free cash.

dividend.title: Realty Income dividend: coverage, yield and outlook
dividend.meta_description: Realty Income's dividend is covered by operating cash and AFFO, with yield, funding needs and risks shaping its outlook.
dividend.opening: Realty Income's declared annualized dividend is $3.258 per share, and operating cash covers the dividend in every year shown. AFFO also covers the dividend under the company's measure, but growth relies on outside funding.
dividend.closing: The full memo also examines Realty Income's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Realty Income pay per share?

paragraphs.text: The dividend starts from the declared annualized rate of $3.258. The base case raises it to $3.32, $3.40 and $3.49, consistent with recent low-single-digit growth and AFFO coverage. The bear case holds it flat at $3.258 because funding pressure could force a pause. The bull case reaches $3.36, $3.50 and $3.65 if per-share AFFO accelerates while coverage remains sound. Q2 payout was 74.5%, leaving room for gradual increases.

blocks.heading: Does Realty Income's dividend come from its cash?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash covered Realty Income’s dividend in every year shown, but it did not cover the company’s full growth program.
The dividend is covered under Realty Income’s AFFO measure, but that cushion is not simply spare cash.

blocks.heading: What could change Realty Income's dividend?

paragraphs.text: The forecast would move toward the bear case if debt refinancing becomes more expensive, acquisition yields fall below funding costs or public equity becomes the main source of investment capital. Those pressures would slow AFFO per share and compress the multiple during 2027–2029.

blocks.heading: What has Realty Income guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Management’s August 2026 outlook calls for AFFO per share of $4.44–$4.45 and $10 billion of investment in 2026. It also targets same-store rent growth of 1.1%–1.3% and 98.5% occupancy.

blocks.heading: Has Realty Income kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: The company achieved the maximum payout on each company-performance objective for 2025. Roy received a 190% score on his individual-performance component. That means he earned 190% of the target for that part of the bonus, not 190% of all compensation. The independent committee made the final decision after considering his recommendations for other executives.

blocks.heading: What have Realty Income’s last eight quarters shown?

paragraphs.text: In the second quarter of 2026, Realty Income reported higher revenue and NOI than in the comparable quarter. FFO per share and AFFO per share also improved, while occupancy remained high. That combination suggests that the business expanded without losing its basic operating stability, although acquisitions and other investments contributed to the larger base.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Realty Income’s next release?

paragraphs.text: The first checkpoint is the third-quarter 2026 report, scheduled after the market closes on November 2. It should show whether investment volume is on pace, AFFO is tracking guidance, and how much earnings still depends on termination receipts. It should also update occupancy, same-store rent growth, credit losses, and cash remaining after dividends.
